name: Executive order of October 3, 1873 cancelling the January 9, 1873 reserve and establishing the Tule River reservation
aka: Tule River reservation, second executive order
nations: Tule River Indian Tribe (Yokuts, with Owens Valley Paiute and Tübatulabal members)
Bands Royce lists as King's River, Owen's River and Tule River Indians
promises: Not a treaty: the President cancelled the reserve of January 9, 1873 and set apart another on the Tule River in its place, from the South Fork of the Tule River 4 miles below the Soda Springs north to the ridge between the North Fork and Middle Fork (Royce).
The Tribe says this order about doubled the reservation, to 91,837 acres, because the January land was unsuited to farming.

breaches.what: The Tule River Tribe says President Hayes's 1878 order cut the reservation back to about its original size and that the President lacked authority under federal law to reduce it; it also says its people on the Madden Farm were forcibly and violently removed to the new reservation in 1876, and claims damages for the 1873 removal and the 1878 reduction.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Tule River Indian Tribe, with the Native American Rights Fund, water settlement presentation, September 24, 2013

source.title: Tule River Indian Tribe Water Settlement (presentation by the Tule River Tribe with the Native American Rights Fund and others, September 24, 2013)
source.publisher: Native American Rights Fund, National Indian Law Library

breaches.quote: The President lacked the authority under federal law to reduced the size of the Reservation.

landTaken: Royce records that the executive order of August 3, 1878 restored part of this reservation to the public domain (area 607) and that the remainder is the present Tule River reserve.
compensation: Nothing paid for the 1878 reduction was found. In 2013 the Tribe put its historical damages for the 1878 reduction at $41.9 million in 2007 dollars; this is the Tribe's claim, not an award.
today: The present Tule River Reservation is 55,396 acres by the Tribe's 2013 count. A bill to ratify the Tribe's 2007 water settlement, S. 689, was reported in the Senate on May 12, 2025; it would have the Tribe waive claims related to the creation or reduction of the Reservation. No record of its enactment was found.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says its first reservation of valley farmland (the Madden Farm) was taken by Indian agents through state patents, that its people were forcibly removed to the mountain reservation in 1876, and that the 1878 reduction was beyond the President's authority.

In 2024 House testimony, Vice Chairman Lester Shine Nieto said the 1856 reservation of about 2,440 acres of valley farmland was partly taken through fraudulent land warrants issued to Indian agents Madden and Benson, which the United States never challenged, that in 1873 the Tribe was forcibly removed to mountainous land it protested, and that the August 1878 executive order unlawfully cut the enlarged 91,837 acre reservation back to about 48,000 acres.

openQuestions: Royce numbers area 607 under the executive order of August 3, 1878: it is the land that order restored to the public domain, partly from the January 9, 1873 reserve and partly from the October 3, 1873 additions. treaties.json gives area 607 to the January 9, 1873, October 3, 1873 and August 3, 1878 entries, and cession-1873-10-03-king-s-river-owen-s-river-tule-river is a second entry for the October 3, 1873 order. Not edited.

Decided by Jordan 2026-11-08: an executive order taking back executive-order land is not a breach by itself; it needs a finding. the 1878 reduction took back land set apart by executive order, not by treaty. Without a court or Commission finding it stays contested, resting on the Tribe's statement that the President lacked authority.
The acreages (48,000 and 91,837 acres in 1873, 55,396 today) come from the Tribe's 2013 presentation, not the orders; the 1878 order states no acreage.
The Indians of California claims (ICC Dockets 31 and 37) covered aboriginal California land generally and were not reviewed for this file.
The Tribe's own website was not found; its 2016 Senate testimony would not download.
treaties.json lists Big Sandy and North Fork Mono rancherias as present-day tribes; their link to this reservation was not checked.
2026-11-08: counted once with cession-1873-10-03-king-s-river-owen-s-river-tule-river (the same October 3, 1873 Tule River order, listed twice). The map still shows this row.

plain.promised: Not a treaty. In October 1873 the President replaced the January reserve with a larger Tule River reservation, about doubled in size, the Tribe says, because the first land was poor for farming.
plain.happened: In 1878 a new order returned part of it to the public domain. The Tribe says the President had no authority to shrink it. No court or claims commission finding was found.
plain.today: The remainder is the Tule River Reservation, 55,396 acres by the Tribe's count. Nothing paid or returned was found; a 2025 water settlement bill had not become law.
